01

How flow cytometry works

The physics you need to explain a strange dot plot to a lab director, in the order the instrument actually does it: fluid, light, signal, plot.

1.1 · The three subsystems

Every flow cytometer — BriCyte included — is three systems working in sequence. The fluidics system carries stained cells one at a time past a laser. The optics system shines lasers on them and collects the light that comes back. The electronics system turns that light into numbers and hands them to the software. Understanding a strange result almost always means asking which of the three is misbehaving.

1.2 · Fluidics: hydrodynamic focusing

Sample is injected into the centre of a fast-moving, laminar sheath flow. Because the sheath stream narrows as it approaches the laser, the sample core is squeezed into a thin single-file thread of cells — this is hydrodynamic focusing. A faster sheath flow makes the sample core narrower (fewer cells side-by-side, better resolution but slower throughput); a slower sheath flow lets the core widen (faster events/second, but coincident cells can be miscounted). On the BriCyte, this is the “Low / Med / High” flow-rate setting: Low ≈ 10 μL/min, Med ≈ 50 μL/min, High ≈ 100 μL/min — use Low for anything where resolution matters more than speed (QC beads, compensation controls).

Field tip

Air bubbles or a sample tube left to run dry are the single most common cause of unstable fluidics — they show up as a sudden shift or scatter in every plot at once, not just one population. Re-run rather than re-gate.

1.3 · Optics: scatter and fluorescence

As a cell crosses the focused laser spot, it scatters light and, if it carries fluorescent antibody, emits fluorescence at a longer wavelength than the exciting light (the Stokes shift). Two scatter signals are collected on every cytometer:

  • Forward scatter (FSC) — collected close to the laser’s axis (roughly 1–10.5° on BriCyte). Roughly tracks cell size; used to separate debris from intact cells.
  • Side scatter (SSC) — collected at ~90° to the beam. Tracks internal complexity/granularity — this is what separates lymphocytes, monocytes and granulocytes on a CD45‑SSC plot even before any antibody is considered.

Fluorescence is filtered through band-pass filters (named by centre/width, e.g. 530/30 passes 515–545 nm) onto dedicated detectors, one per colour channel.

Fluorochromes used in this panel

Marker : fluorochromeLaserFilterEx maxEm max
CD3 FITCBlue 488 nm530/30494 nm520 nm
CD8 PEBlue 488 nm585/40565 nm575 nm
CD45 PerCPBlue 488 nm690/50482 nm675 nm
CD4 APCRed 638 nm660/20650 nm660 nm

1.4 · Compensation

Fluorochrome emission spectra overlap — some FITC photons always leak into the PE detector, and vice versa. Compensation mathematically subtracts that spillover so each detector reports only its own dye. BriCyte does this automatically during QC/auto‑setup against the QC beads, but it can be reviewed or fine-tuned per sample on the Compensation tab (input range 0–200%). A panel that looks “smeared” diagonally on a two-colour plot, rather than in tight rectangular quadrants, is almost always a compensation problem, not a biological one.

1.5 · Gating

Gating isolates the population you care about by drawing a region around it and asking the software to only look inside that region on the next plot. The standard sequence for this panel is: scatter/CD45 (find lymphocytes) → CD3 vs CD4 and CD3 vs CD8 (quadrant/cross gates for T‑cell subsets). Section 7 covers exactly how to verify each gate is sitting correctly before a report goes out.

1.6 · Pulse height, width and area

Each detector doesn’t just report one number — it reports a pulse as a cell crosses the beam. Height is the peak signal; area is roughly height × width and approximates total light collected; width tracks how long the cell took to cross the beam (its time of flight). Width is the classic tool for spotting doublets — two cells stuck together give a wider pulse than one cell, even when their total fluorescence (area) looks similar.

02

The BriCyte platform

BriCyte E6 launched in 2014 and has 900+ installations, including 300+ Class A tertiary hospitals in mainland China; BriCyte MX followed in 2024 as the 3‑laser, up-to-14-colour successor. MC sits between them on the optics side. All three run the same MRFlow software and the same CD3/CD4/CD8/CD45 panel logic.

BriCyte MX carries up to 3 lasers (blue 488 nm / 50 mW, red 638 nm / 55 mW, violet 405 nm / 100 mW); BriCyte MC carries blue and red only. Filters are user-replaceable without re-calibrating the optical bench.

2.3 · Sample loading modes

2.4 · Fourth-generation absolute counting

Older systems need a reference microsphere added to the tube to convert a percentage into an absolute cell count (cells/μL), or a mechanical metering pump. BriCyte instead uses a flow sensor to directly measure sample volume delivered, giving percentage and absolute count from the same tube without added beads:

GenerationMethod
1stDual platform (separate hematology count + flow %)
2ndReference microspheres added to the tube
3rdMetering pump
4th — BriCyteFlow sensor (≈0.5 nL/min precision) — no microspheres, no added consumable cost, no clog risk from beads

In head-to-head studies, BC‑700 hematology lymphocyte counts correlated tightly with BriCyte MX absolute counts, and BriCyte E6/MX percentage and absolute-count results correlated well against BD FACSCalibur, BD FACSCanto II, BD FACSLyric and Beckman Coulter DxFlex (R² typically 0.98–0.99 across CD3+, CD3+CD4+ and CD3+CD8+) in the studies cited in the vendor training material — treat these as manufacturer-supplied comparative data, not an independent verification.

2.5 · Supported panels

  • Lymphocyte Subsets (T/B/NK‑Auto) — two tubes, T and BNK, reporting T/B/NK percentages, absolute counts and CD4/CD8 ratio
  • T Lymphocyte Subsets (CD3/8/45/4‑Auto) — this guide’s panel, single tube
  • HLA‑B27‑Auto — see §8
03

The T-cell panel

CD3‑FITC/CD8‑PE/CD45‑PerCP/CD4‑APC Reagent — a single four-colour cocktail that identifies T lymphocytes and their two major subsets in one tube.

3.1 · What each marker is doing

MarkerMWWhat it identifies
CD320–30 kDaε chain of the T‑cell receptor complex — defines the T‑lymphocyte population
CD455 kDaHelper/inducer T‑cells; binds MHC‑II; the major HIV receptor
CD832 kDaSuppressor/cytotoxic T‑cells; binds MHC‑I
CD45180–220 kDaLeukocyte Common Antigen — expressed on all leukocytes; used to gate the lymphocyte population on CD45 vs SSC before any subset analysis

CD4 and CD8 percentages are not perfectly exclusive: CD8 also reacts with NK cells, and CD4 also reacts with monocytes — which is exactly why the CD45/SSC lymphocyte gate has to be drawn correctly before either quadrant plot is read (§7).

3.2 · Clinical use

CD4+ counts monitor disease progression and treatment efficacy in HIV infection — CD4 testing remains central to the 90‑90‑90 HIV treatment targets, especially in HIV–tuberculosis co‑infected patients. CD8+ counts outside the reference range are associated with certain autoimmune conditions. More broadly, T‑lymphocyte subset testing is used for:

  • Direction and monitoring of infection, including more than two serial results to gauge treatment response
  • Immunodeficiency work-up — recurrent/severe infection, or before paediatric vaccination in a child with a suspicious history
  • Screening for haematological disease/lymphoma when prolonged treatment for another condition is not working as expected
  • Oncology — treatment-effectiveness monitoring and infection-risk assessment during therapy
  • Peri-operative infection-risk assessment
  • Monitoring patients on immunosuppressants for complications of low immunity
  • General health-screening / sub-health assessment

Who should be tested: patients with recurrent or severe infections or infections resistant to conventional treatment; patients with allergic, autoimmune or autoinflammatory disease; patients with haematological or solid tumours; patients with a family history of immunodeficiency; and patients on long-term immunosuppressive therapy.

3.3 · Specimen requirements

Anticoagulant

K2‑ or K3‑EDTA venous blood

Minimum volume

200 μL (follow the tube manufacturer’s own minimum fill line first)

Stain within

48 h of draw, stored at 20–25°C — do not refrigerate or freeze

Acquire within

24 h of staining

Ideal WBC concentration is (3–10)×10³ cells/μL — outside that range, concentrate or dilute the specimen first (a Mindray hematology analyzer WBC count, e.g. BC‑5800/BC‑5380, is the recommended check).

Interfering conditions

Refrigerated-before-staining blood, samples from patients on immunosuppressive drugs (poor population resolution), circulating blast cells, hyperbilirubinemia, chylous (lipemic) specimens and hemolysed specimens can all distort results. Reject and redraw grossly lipemic, jaundiced, haemolysed or clotted specimens rather than trying to salvage them.

3.4 · Instrument compatibility

Validated on Mindray BriCyte MX/MC/E6, BD FACSCalibur, BD FACSCanto II and BD FACSLyric; the cytometer must provide 488 nm and 635/638 nm excitation and four-colour (FITC/PE/PerCP/APC) detection of scatter plus fluorescence.

3.5 · Reference ranges & result logic

95% reference range, n=210 (114 M / 96 F), hematologically normal adults 18–65y, China — establish your own local range
SubsetRange
CD3+ T lymphocytes49.6–84.4%
CD3+CD4+ helper/inducer21.1–50.6%
CD3+CD8+ suppressor/cytotoxic13.7–46.9%

Report logic: (CD3+CD4+%) + (CD3+CD8+%) should equal CD3+% within a 5–10% deviation. Outside that window, consider an excess of an atypical T‑cell subset (TCR‑γδ+, CD3+CD4–CD8–, or CD3+CD4+CD8dim) rather than assuming an assay error — see the review checklist in §7.

3.6 · Documented performance

Correlation vs BD Multitest CD3/CD8/CD45/CD4 (BD Multitest IMK kit), whole blood, n=44
SubsetR, BriCyte E6R, BD Canto IIR, BD FACSCalibur
CD3+%0.9960.9890.985
CD3+CD4+%0.9940.9910.980
CD3+CD8+%0.9980.9920.991

Linearity (BriCyte E6): CD3+ 32–20,818 cells/μL · CD3+CD4+ 6–2,856 cells/μL · CD3+CD8+ 12–13,641 cells/μL. Within-specimen CVs in the manufacturer’s precision study ran 1.1–3.2% across the three subsets on BriCyte E6.

Limitations

Clinical reference only — combine with symptoms, history and other lab results before a diagnosis is made. Not intended to screen for leukemic cells or to phenotype leukemia specimens. Results are not comparable across laboratories using different manufacturers’ equipment. Race, gender, age and preparative technique can all shift the reference range, which is why every laboratory is expected to verify or establish its own.

04

Sample prep & staining

The Lyse/No‑Wash protocol used for this panel — identical whether you learned it from the reagent’s IFU, the training deck, or the laboratory’s own SOP; the three agree step for step.

What you need

  • CD3‑FITC/CD8‑PE/CD45‑PerCP/CD4‑APC reagent, 12×75 mm flow tubes, EDTA whole blood
  • 1× Lysing Solution, freshly diluted 1:10 with distilled/deionized water (never isotonic saline or PBS — it will not lyse)
  • Vortex mixer, calibrated micropipettes (20 μL / 50 μL / 450 μL)
  1. Label one tube “T.” Pipette 20 μL of CD3‑FITC/CD8‑PE/CD45‑PerCP/CD4‑APC reagent into the bottom of the tube.
  2. Add blood. Pipette 50 μL of well‑mixed EDTA whole blood into the bottom of the tube — add the antibody first, then the blood, and avoid smearing it on the tube wall (wipe with a cotton swab if it happens). For absolute counting, invert the blood tube 10× before drawing, and consider reverse pipetting for accuracy.
  3. Mix & incubate #1. Gentle point-vortex 3–5×. Incubate 15 minutes at room temperature (20–25°C), protected from light.
  4. Lyse. Add 450 μL of freshly diluted 1× Lysing Solution. Gentle point-vortex 3–5×.
  5. Incubate #2. 10–15 minutes at room temperature, protected from light — the red cells lyse while leukocytes are preserved and fixed.
  6. Mix and run. Mix gently immediately before loading to prevent aggregation. If not tested immediately, hold in the dark at room temperature and complete acquisition within 24 h of staining.
Pre-treatment checklist
  • EDTA or heparin anticoagulant only — reject and redraw severe lipemia/jaundice/hemolysis/clots
  • Antibody goes into the tube first, blood second
  • Return antibody reagent to 2–8°C immediately after use
  • Dilute lysing solution with distilled water only — isotonic saline or PBS will not lyse red cells
  • If ambient temperature is low, incubate in a 37°C block or water bath (foil the tube mouth for a water bath)
  • Open/manual-loading samples must be mixed by hand immediately before the run

The companion BNK tube (for context)

Where the laboratory also runs the full T/B/NK panel, a second tube (“BNK”) is prepared the same way with CD3‑FITC/CD16+56‑PE/CD45‑PerCP/CD19‑APC reagent, 20 μL reagent + 50 μL blood, same incubation times. The two tubes are cross-checked against each other during review — see §7.2.

Lyse/Wash alternative (when a washed, fixed specimen is needed instead)
1Add 2 mL of 1× Lysing Solution to 100 μL blood+antibody; vortex; incubate 10 min, dark, room temp
2Centrifuge 5 min at 300×g; discard supernatant
3Resuspend in 2 mL PBS; repeat the centrifuge/discard step
4Resuspend the pellet in an appropriate buffer for analysis (fixed specimens are stable a few hours — analyse within 2 h if unfixed)
05

Running the test

The MRFlow software workflow, from power-on to shutdown, for the T‑Lymphocyte Subsets (CD3/8/45/4‑Auto) template.

5.1 · Start of day

  1. Power on the cytometer at the rear switch; confirm the status indicator settles to Ready (steady, not flickering). A blue/yellow or blue/red flicker means the software/hardware environment is abnormal — contact Mindray support rather than proceeding.
  2. Start the computer and open MRFlow (default password Admin — configure real user IDs under Settings per your laboratory’s access policy).
  3. Let the instrument complete its initialization sequence.
  4. Run daily QC before any patient sample — see §6.

5.2 · Placing a sample order

  1. On the Sample screen, select Sample Orders.
  2. Enter the Sample ID (auto-increments; max 25 characters including prefix). For batch autoload runs, set the tube position and order number.
  3. In Panels, choose T Lymphocyte Subsets (CD3/8/45/4‑Auto) — the software adds the tube automatically.
  4. Select Submit.

On a Mindray template you may only adjust Abs. Count settings, stop conditions/events and report text/reference ranges before the run completes — the gating logic itself is locked to keep results comparable across operators.

5.3 · Loading & acquisition

Manual loading

  1. Place the prepared tube on the sample probe holder.
  2. Select the tube, adjust voltage/threshold/compensation only if genuinely needed, and start acquisition.
  3. Watch the plots populate in real time; stop conditions (time, volume, or events in a set gate, combined as “OR”) end the run automatically.

Autoloading

  1. Load tubes into the carousel matching the work order, starting at the correct position — the system only reads tubes downstream of the designated start tube.
  2. Close the autoloader door and confirm the carousel seats correctly.
  3. Start the batch; the instrument aspirates, analyses and advances automatically.

Typical flow-rate settings: Low ≈10 μL/min (best resolution — use for QC beads), Medium ≈50 μL/min, High ≈100 μL/min (routine throughput).

5.4 · Reviewing and releasing

Once acquisition finishes, gates can still be dragged and the statistics recalculate live — do this before printing/transmitting, following the checklist in §7. Reports can be printed or sent directly to the LIS/HIS from the report preview screen.

5.5 · End of day / shutdown

  1. Select the shutdown icon in the top-right of the software.
  2. Prepare two tubes: ≥3 mL of diluted Probe Cleanser (1:10 in distilled water) in position 1, and ≥3 mL distilled water in position 2.
  3. Confirm to run the shutdown program — it completes automatically.
  4. Once the status indicator turns yellow, power off at the rear switch, empty the waste container appropriately, and power down the computer and monitor.
Note

After shutdown, wait at least 60 seconds before powering back on. Avoid cycling power repeatedly in a short window — it can damage the instrument.

06

Quality control

Two layers of QC: auto setup calibrates the instrument itself every day using QC fluorescent beads, and panel QC (whole blood QC) validates the entire process — staining, lysis, instrument and analysis — using an assigned-value blood control.

6.1 · Daily auto setup with QC beads

The QC particle is SPHERO™ Supra/Ultra Rainbow Fluorescent Particles (Mindray catalogue equivalent 105‑004485‑00, Spherotech URFP‑30‑2 / SRCP‑35‑2A, 3.0–3.5 μm, ≈10×10&sup6; particles/mL). Every particle carries a mixture of fluorophores excitable from 365–650 nm, so one bead lot can set every channel on every laser at once.

  1. Shake/vortex the bead vial. Add 1–2 drops into a tube with 1 mL sheath fluid; mix well.
  2. First time with a new lot: QC → QC Setup → QC Particles → New — scan the lot’s three QR codes, or enter the lot number, product ID and channel targets manually.
  3. Place the bead solution in the loading position. QC → Auto Setup; choose the lot; choose System Calibration + Voltage Calibration for a full setup, or Voltage Calibration alone for a quick recheck; start the test.
  4. Confirm every laser/channel shows a pass indicator on the report before running any patient sample. A repeated failure is escalated to Mindray for recalibration — do not analyse patient samples on a failed setup.
  5. Review the Levey‑Jennings trend under QC → QC Graph → QC Particles for long-term drift, not just today’s pass/fail.
Do not skip

Running a QC sample while an unrelated instrument error is showing produces unreliable calibration. Clear all errors first, then run QC.

6.2 · Panel (whole blood) QC

Stain and lyse the assigned-value blood control exactly as a patient sample (§4), run it under the matching QC panel template, and let the software plot the result against the control’s target value and limits on a Levey‑Jennings chart.

  1. QC → QC Setup → Whole Blood QC → New — enter control name, lot, expiry and product ID; choose the panel template; set target values/limits (or upper & lower limit) per parameter.
  2. Prepare and stain the control per its own instructions, using the same lyse/no-wash steps as §4.
  3. Place a QC sample order using the QC panel template, then run it exactly as a normal sample (§5).
  4. Adjust compensation/gates only if genuinely needed to correctly classify the populations.
  5. Review results under QC → QC Graph → Whole Blood QC.

6.3 · Levey‑Jennings / Westgard-style QC rules

RuleTriggerClass
1‑2sOne result beyond ±2SDWarning
1‑3sOne result beyond ±3SDOut of control
2‑2sTwo consecutive results (or two QC samples at once) beyond the same ±2SDOut of control
4‑1sFour consecutive results (or two consecutive from two QC samples) beyond the same ±1SDOut of control
10‑xTen consecutive results (or five from two QC samples) on one side of targetOut of control
R‑4sOne QC sample >+2SD while another <–2SDOut of control

QC point colour convention: green between ±2SD (in control), amber between ±2SD and ±3SD (warning), red beyond ±3SD (out of control).

6A

Calibration refresh

“Refreshing” the calibration happens at two levels on the BriCyte MX/MC: the daily auto setup (voltage, fluorescence compensation and laser delay time, reset from QC beads) and the rare absolute count calibration factor (the number that converts events to cells/μL). They answer different questions, so know which one you need before you touch the instrument.

In plain words

Think of a kitchen scale. Auto setup is zeroing the scale every morning with a known weight. Here the known weight is the QC bead: the instrument tunes its detectors until the beads read the way they should. Do it every day.

The absolute count factor is a different thing. It is the number that turns “events the instrument counted” into “cells per microlitre”. It is set at the factory, so leave it alone unless a key part was replaced, the instrument sat in storage, or QC says something is wrong.

To refresh it, count the same fresh blood on a trusted reference device and on the BriCyte, then scale the factor by how far apart the two answers are. Three runs each are averaged, so one odd run does not move the result.

6A.1 · Which refresh do I need?

RefreshWhat it resetsRun it when…Where
Auto setup
Routine		Detector voltages, fluorescence compensation, delay time (red vs blue/violet laser)Before running samples on any day you use Mindray templates; a quick Voltage Calibration recheck after a drift or errorQC → Auto Setup
Absolute count factor
Rare		The absolute count calibration factor (allowed range 50–150%)A major part is replaced (flow cell, sample probe, flow sensor); the instrument returns to use after long-term storage; or QC suggests a problemSetup → Host Setup

The factor is calibrated at the factory for the Lymphocyte Subsets auto algorithm (Mindray template). Do not change it just because one result looks odd.

6A.2 · Refresh 1 — daily auto setup

Full steps are in §6.1. The refresh itself is short:

  1. Clear any instrument error first — calibrating with an error showing gives unreliable results.
  2. Prepare fresh QC particle solution on the day: 1–2 drops of QC fluorescence particles in 1 mL sheath fluid; keep it in the dark.
  3. Load it, open QC → Auto Setup, pick the lot, and choose System Calibration + Voltage Calibration (full) or Voltage Calibration (quick).
  4. Start the test, then open the System Calibration and Voltage Calibration report tabs. Every laser/channel must show the pass indicator.
  5. If it fails: check for operator error and retry. Repeated failure → contact Mindray service; do not run patient samples.

6A.3 · Refresh 2 — absolute count calibration factor

Before you start

The instrument must be in normal working status and meet its basic performance specs — carryover, forward-scatter resolution and side-scatter resolution (manual Appendix A.8). Passing auto setup first is the practical way to confirm this. Wear PPE; fresh blood is biohazardous.

Choose one of two reference methods. Both end the same way: compute a new factor and type it into Setup → Host Setup → Absolute Count Calibration.

Method A · Lymphocyte concentration

  1. Take a normal fresh blood sample with lymphocytes of 1,500–3,000 events/μL.
  2. Run it 3× in a row on a calibrated hematology analyzer (QC in control) or another traceable flow cytometer. The mean is the Reference Mean.
  3. On the BriCyte: Abs. Count tab → tick Enable absolute count. Run 3 lymphocyte counts at high flow rate, 1 min each. The mean is the Measured Mean.
  4. Read the Current Calibration Factor from Setup → Host Setup and calculate the new one.
  5. Enter the new factor in Absolute Count Calibration.

New factor = Current factor × Reference Mean ÷ Measured Mean

Method B · BD TruCOUNT beads

  1. Add 50 μL fresh blood to a TruCOUNT tube (not touching the wall).
  2. Add 450 μL 1× lysing solution, vortex gently, incubate 15 min, 20–25°C, in the dark.
  3. Create a custom template with correct gates for the TruCOUNT beads.
  4. Abs. Count tab → Enable absolute count, Dilution ratio 1:10. Run 3 counts at high flow rate, 1 min each; the mean is the Measured Mean.
  5. Take the bead target value from the tube pack; Reference Beads Concentration = target ÷ 500 (events/μL).
  6. Calculate and enter the new factor as below.

New factor = Current factor × Reference Beads Conc. ÷ Measured Mean

6A.4 · Factor calculator

Does the arithmetic and the range check from the formulas above. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere. Values here are for working out the number; you still enter it in the instrument yourself.

Worked example (illustrative numbers): current 100%, Reference Mean 2,100, Measured Mean 1,890 → 100 × 2,100 ÷ 1,890 = 111.1%. The cytometer was under-counting by about 10%, so the factor goes up.

6A.5 · If the result is invalid or doesn’t hold

  • Factor outside 50–150% (or the software flags it): it is invalid. Look for the cause — sample not mixed thoroughly, bead sample stuck to the tube wall, wrong dilution ratio, wrong target value — then repeat the whole run and recalculate.
  • Still out of range after a clean repeat: stop and contact the Mindray Customer Service Department or your local distributor.
  • Auto setup keeps failing: same escalation — Mindray recalibrates the instrument.
Suggested follow-up (field practice, not from the manual)

After changing the factor, run a panel QC (§6.2) and a fresh normal sample, and confirm the absolute counts agree with the reference method before releasing patient results. Record the old and new factor, date, reason and operator in the site’s instrument log.

Not the same “refresh”

The refresh button in the analysis control area only redraws the plots so populations sit properly (and Auto Voltage Adjustment redraws after it resets voltages). It does not calibrate anything.

Source: BriCyte MX/MC Operator’s Manual H‑046‑029192 — §6.2.4 (absolute count calibration factor, 6.2.4.1 and 6.2.4.2) and §9.2 (auto setup).

6B

QC beads: 30-2 and 35-2A

What the QC bead is, how it is used every day, how the two Spherotech beads in your files compare, and the original datasheets.

In plain words

A rainbow bead is a tiny plastic ball (about 3 µm) dyed with a mixture of many fluorescent dyes. Because the dye mixture is in every bead, a single bead glows in every detector, from violet to far red. It works like a colour chart where every colour sits on one patch.

The beads are almost identical to each other, so they make a good ruler. Each morning Auto Setup tunes every detector until the bead reads its target value, then records the setting. If the beads read differently next week, the Levey‑Jennings chart shows the drift before patient results are affected.

You have datasheets for two Spherotech beads: URFP‑30‑2 (“Ultra”) and SRCP‑35‑2A (“Supra, mid-range”). Both are sold for routine calibration of flow cytometers.

6B.1 · The two beads side by side

URFP‑30‑2 (Ultra) SRCP‑35‑2A (Supra, Mid‑Range) Same on both sheets

ItemURFP‑30‑2 (file “302”)SRCP‑35‑2A (file “352a”)
Product nameSPHERO™ Ultra Rainbow Fluorescent ParticlesSPHERO™ Supra Rainbow Fluorescent Particles, Mid-Range
Catalog no.URFP‑30‑2SRCP‑35‑2A
Size3.0–3.4 µm3.0–3.59 µm
Special featureEnhanced UV and far-red fluorescence intensity“Mid-Range” in the name only; the sheet gives no detail
Suggested dilution1–2 drops in 1 mL3–5 drops in 1 mL
Sample lot (pack 2 mL)MAN01AM01
Datasheet extraPage 2: nine histograms (lot MAN01)Page 1 only

Source: Spherotech technical data sheets 941‑3373E (URFP‑30‑2) and 941‑5353A (SRCP‑35‑2A).

Check before relying on either bead

1. Both datasheets say “for research applications only, not for diagnostic use”. 2. The BriCyte manual says to use only the Mindray-specified control and does not name either bead, so confirm with Mindray which one your lab should use. 3. For drops per mL, follow the BriCyte manual (1–2 drops in 1 mL). The 35-2A sheet suggests 3–5 drops for general flow cytometry.

6B.2 · Intended use: what the sheets say and what I infer

URFP‑30‑2 · Ultra

On the datasheet

  • Routine calibration of flow cytometers
  • Enhanced UV and far-red fluorescence intensity
  • 1–2 drops in 1 mL
  • Has a page of histograms for lot MAN01

My reading (inference)

  • A brighter bead for the channels excited by the violet (405 nm) and red (638 nm) lasers
  • Fits a 3-laser BriCyte MX where violet and far-red channels need enough signal to reach target

SRCP‑35‑2A · Supra, Mid‑Range

On the datasheet

  • Routine calibration of flow cytometers
  • “Mid-Range” in the product name, not explained
  • 3–5 drops in 1 mL
  • Slightly wider size range (3.0–3.59 µm)

My reading (inference)

  • A medium-brightness general-purpose bead
  • Needing more drops per mL hints it is dimmer per drop, but the sheet does not say
Which one do I use?

Neither datasheet assigns a different job to the beads. On the BriCyte, the deciding factors are the bead the manual allows (the Mindray-specified control) and the QC lot target values that load when you scan the lot’s three QR codes (§6.1). Ask Mindray which bead and lot your instrument is set up for, and Spherotech for the intensity specification behind “Ultra” and “Mid-Range”.

6B.3 · Original datasheets

07

Gate & result review

This is the checklist that turns raw dot plots into a defensible report — the same sequence the SOP and the training material both walk through, verbatim.

7.1 · Verify the gates, in order

  1. CD45 vs SSC (tube T). The lymphocyte gate must tightly and accurately encircle the lymphocyte cluster — low SSC, positive CD45, clearly separated from monocytes (higher SSC) and granulocytes (broader, highest SSC).
  2. CD3 vs CD4, and CD3 vs CD8 cross-gates. The horizontal line sits just above the double-negative and CD3-only clusters without cutting into either; the vertical line sits centred between the double-negative/CD3-only clusters and the single/double-positive clusters, with all four quadrants clearly separated.

7.2 · Internal consistency checks

  • T vs BNK tube CD3% agreement (where both tubes are run): should be within 5% of each other. A larger gap usually means a sample/tube mix-up, not a biological finding — re-check tube labelling before re-testing.
  • CD4% + CD8% vs CD3%: should agree within 5–10%. Beyond that threshold, work through the branching check below.
  • T+B+NK sum (T/B/NK panel): should total 95–105% in a normal individual; no prompt needed above 90%. Below 90%, inspect for an abnormal/atypical population and note its phenotype and percentage, or (if none is visible) note a CD3–CD19–CD16–CD56– population. The automated Mindray algorithm will not itself report a sum above 105%.
  • First-plot screen. Compare the very first plot of each tube (typically FSC/SSC or CD45/SSC) against the normal reference image. More than 10% of events sitting in the primitive/blast-cell region is reported as a peripheral-blood blast-cell suspicion, not silently passed through.

7.3 · When CD45/SSC is clean but the CD3/CD4/CD8 plots are not

If lymphocytes gate cleanly on CD45 vs SSC but the downstream CD3‑CD4 / CD3‑CD8 plots show poor, disorderly separation, the cause is usually residual protein/debris interfering with antibody resolution — wash and re-suspend the tube:

  1. Add 2 mL sheath fluid to the prepared T (and BNK) tube; mix gently on the vortex.
  2. Centrifuge at 1,500 rpm for 5 minutes.
  3. Remove the supernatant in one pour — never a second pour, and never shake the tube while decanting.
  4. Add 500 μL sheath fluid to resuspend the pellet, then re-run on the instrument.
After a wash step

The instrument’s absolute count from a washed tube is no longer reliable — report absolute counts using the CBC lymphocyte count × the flow cytometry percentage instead: Lymphocyte count (CBC) × subset %.

7.4 · Release checklist

  • Gates verified per §7.1 on every tube
  • Internal consistency checks per §7.2 within tolerance, or an explanatory note added
  • No unexplained blast/primitive-cell signal >10%
  • QC for the day is in control (§6)

Only once all four are satisfied should the report be printed or transmitted to LIS/HIS.

7A

Plot types & display scale

What you can draw in MRFlow, how to add and edit a plot, and how each fluorescence axis is scaled (linear, log or biexponential). Everything here is from the BriCyte MX/MC Operator’s Manual, §3.6.1 and §6.7.

In plain words

A plot is a picture of your cells. A histogram uses one marker: bar height shows how many cells have each brightness. A dot plot uses two markers: every dot is one cell placed on an X–Y map. Contour and density plots show the same map but mark where cells crowd together instead of drawing every dot. A 3D plot adds a third marker.

The display scale is how the axis ruler is stretched. Linear spaces numbers evenly. Log makes each step ten times bigger, so very dim and very bright cells both fit. Biexponential is log for bright signals but linear near zero, so cells with almost no signal (or slightly negative after compensation) stay visible instead of piling on the axis.

In the manual’s own screenshots, FSC and SSC are drawn on a linear 0–1M axis and the fluorescence markers on log decades from 10¹ to 10⁶.

7A.1 · Plot types

Plot typeParametersTypical use in this panel
Histogram1One marker at a time; also the only type that can be overlaid
Dot plot2FSC vs SSC, CD45 vs SSC, CD3 vs CD4 / CD8; the type used by auto voltage and auto compensation
Contour plot2Same axes as a dot plot, drawn as density lines (number of lines is a setting)
Density plot2Same axes, shaded by event density
3D plot3Three markers at once

Plot types and parameter counts: manual Table 3-4. The “typical use” column is application guidance, not manual text.

7A.2 · Adding and editing a plot

Standard add

  1. Choose the plot type on the analysis toolbar.
  2. In the new plot window pick the Data source (default All Events), then the X dimension and Y dimension.

Quick add

  1. Double-click a gate (for example Lym in plot P1).
  2. A new plot appears with the same dimensions as the parent plot and the gate as its data source.

To change a plot afterwards, open its X or Y dimension drop-down and pick another parameter. Plots can be copied and pasted in the work area or copied to the clipboard.

7A.3 · Display scale per channel

Each fluorescence channel is shown in one of three ways. FSC and SSC are enabled by default. Set the mode on the Channels tab of the cytometer control area, together with the voltage.

Display scaleMin valueMax valueNotes
Linear0 – 1,048,5750 – 1,048,575Raw signal range
Log1.00 – 6.023.00 – 6.02Values are in decades; 6.02 ≈ 106.02 ≈ 1,048,576
Biexponential1.00 (fixed)3.00 – 6.02Minimum cannot be changed. Negative range is set on the Biexponential tab

Set a channel’s display range

  1. Select the arrow behind the channel and choose Set display ranges of channel dims.
  2. Enter the minimum and maximum, or use the slider. Allowed values depend on the scale (table above).
  3. Choose an application rule: current channel of the current tube, the same dimension across all tubes of the sample, or all dimensions of the sample.
  4. To undo: Reset restores that channel; Reset all restores every channel of every tube under the sample.

Biexponential negative range

The default method is Auto, and the negative range cannot be edited. Select Manual to enable the Below Zero fields; the allowed negative value is 5 – 1,048,575. Biexponential is useful when compensation pushes events below zero and a log axis would pile them against the axis.

Overlay limit

Histogram overlays (up to 5, same dimension, same sample) cannot be built from histograms displayed in biexponential mode. Use log or linear for those.

7A.4 · Display settings in Setup

Under Setup → Para. Setup (select Save after each change):

  • Histogram Smooth — smoothed histogram curves.
  • Show population percentage — percentage label on populations.
  • Background of Histogram — pick the histogram background color.
  • Contour Line Number — how many contour lines a contour plot draws.
  • Frequent data type — A, H or A&H: which signals (area / height) are unfolded in the dimension lists. Width (W) stays folded.
Auto compensation default

For the Auto_Compensation template, choosing signal A applies biexponential to all fluorescence channels; choosing H applies log.

Source: Operator’s Manual §3.6.1.1–3.6.1.3, §6.7.1, §6.7.2, §6.7.4, §8.3.3.5.

7B

Gate types & managing gates

Seven gate tools are available on the analysis toolbar, and five ways to manage a gate once it is drawn. Source: Operator’s Manual §3.6.2.

In plain words

A gate is a fence you draw around a group of cells on a plot. The software then counts only the cells inside the fence and can send them to the next plot, for example the lymphocyte gate feeding the CD3/CD4 plot. There are seven fence shapes to choose from.

Managing gates means what you can do with a fence after drawing it: copy it, paste it onto another plot, overwrite an old one, synchronize it across the tubes of one sample, or delete it. Deleting is the one to be careful with, because plots built from that gate fall back to All Events.

7B.1 · The seven gate types

#Gate typeHow you draw it
1BifurcatedClick one position in the plot; the gate splits there
2Line segmentClick the start, drag, click the end
3Four-quadrantClick one position; it becomes the center point
4RectangleClick the start, drag to the end
5EllipseClick the start, drag to the end
6PolygonClick several positions; the first and last vertex must coincide
7AutopolygonClick a population; the software outlines it

Populations inside a gate are filled with color automatically. Gates are named by type and order of adding (P1, P2…).

7B.2 · Managing gates

Right-click a gate (or the target plot) to open the context menu.

ActionWhat it doesWatch for
DeleteSelect the gate, press Delete or Backspace, or choose Delete from the menuThe gate’s population and statistics are deleted too. If other plots use it as their data source, a confirmation appears; on OK those plots and overlays switch to All Events, and affected custom parameters are deleted
Copy gateRight-click the gate, choose Copy gate—
Paste gateRight-click the target plot, choose Paste gateAdds the copy to that plot
Overwrite gateRight-click the gate to replace, choose Overwrite gateNeeds a copied gate of the same type. The name stays (for example P1)
Synchronize gatesMake gates on other tubes of the same sample match this tube in shape and positionOnly gates with the same name, dimensions, data source and type are synchronized

Synchronize one gate or all gates

Example: Tube 1 and Tube 2 both have a FSC-H vs SSC-H dot plot of All Events, each with polygon P1, ellipse P2 and rectangle P3.

  1. One gate: right-click polygon P1 on Tube 1 and choose Synchronize gates. P1 on Tube 2 takes the same shape and position.
  2. All gates on the plot: right-click blank space on the Tube 1 plot and choose Synchronize gates. Every gate on the matching Tube 2 plot is adjusted.
Before you delete a gate

Check whether another plot is built from it (Quick add makes this common). Deleting the parent resets those plots to All Events, so their populations change.

Gates can also be moved while you tune voltage, threshold and compensation (§7 setup steps). Source: Operator’s Manual §3.6.2, Tables 3-5 and 3-6, §3.6.2.1–3.6.2.3.

08

HLA-B27 add-on

Runs on the same BriCyte hardware and lysing solution as the T-cell panel, with its own two-colour reagent and interpretation logic — worth knowing well since it’s frequently ordered alongside, or instead of, the T-cell panel in the same laboratories.

8.1 · What it is and who orders it

HLA‑B27 is a class I MHC gene product expressed on all nucleated cells, especially abundant on lymphocytes. A positive result does not itself diagnose disease; a negative result largely rules out ankylosing spondylitis.

Positivity rate by condition
ConditionHLA‑B27+
Ankylosing spondylitis≈90%
Reactive arthritis40–80%
Inflammatory bowel disease arthritis35–75%
Psoriatic arthritis40–50%
Undifferentiated spondyloarthropathy≈70%
Acute anterior uveitis (iritis)≈50%
Healthy population≈8%

Typical candidates: family members of an ankylosing-spondylitis patient, patients with unexplained foot/hand joint problems, and people with long-term sedentary occupational postures. Clinically: a negative test largely excludes ankylosing spondylitis; a positive test prompts the clinician to look for additional spondyloarthropathy features before confirming the diagnosis.

8.2 · Sample prep

  1. Two tubes. Tube 1 (isotype control): 20 μL IgG2a‑FITC/IgG1‑PE. Tube 2 (test): 20 μL HLA‑B27‑FITC/HLA‑B7‑PE.
  2. Add 100 μL mixed EDTA venous blood to each tube (avoid the tube wall; wipe with a swab if it happens).
  3. Vortex gently; incubate 15 min at room temperature (20–25°C), dark.
  4. Add 2 mL of freshly diluted 1× lysing solution to each tube; vortex gently; incubate 10 min, room temperature, dark (avoid prolonging this step — extended hemolysin contact can destroy leukocytes).
  5. Centrifuge 1,500 rpm × 5 min; discard supernatant. Add 2 mL sheath fluid, vortex gently to resuspend, centrifuge again 1,500 rpm × 5 min; discard supernatant.
  6. Resuspend in 500 μL sheath fluid. Test within 2 hours.
Wash chemistry

Lysing must be done with distilled water — never isotonic saline or PBS. The wash step, by contrast, must use an isotonic solution (sheath fluid, saline or PBS) — never plain water.

8.3 · Reading the result

  1. Review both FSC‑SSC plots first: lymphocytes must be clearly demarcated from debris, and the gate must accurately circle the lymphocyte cluster, in both the isotype-control tube and the sample tube.
  2. Check the reported MFI shift against the reagent’s cutoff (MFI cutoff 5,400; grey zone 4,860–5,940, i.e. ±10% of cutoff).
  3. Negative — release as reported.
  4. Positive — go back to the sample-tube HLA‑B27/HLA‑B7 plot:
    • Q4 (B27‑single‑positive) > 80% → report positive.
    • Q4 < 80% with double-positive cells present in Q2 → report positive, and note possible HLA‑B7 cross-reactivity; recommend genetic confirmation.
    • Q4 < 80% with cells present in Q1 → report positive, note possible interference, recommend genetic confirmation.
  5. Result in the grey zone (MFI difference within cutoff ±10%) — report the actual value with a note that it falls in the reagent’s grey zone and recommend correlating with another methodology.
  6. “Undetermined” or blank result — lymphocytes were not separated from debris on the scatter plot:
    • If they can be manually re-gated in FSC‑SSC, re-circle the lymphocyte population in both tubes and the result will resolve.
    • If they genuinely cannot be separated, re-prep the sample: check whether the tube looks reddish (incomplete hemolysis — revisit the lysing step), or whether lymphocyte/monocyte/granulocyte numbers look normal on FSC‑SSC (if abnormally low, hemolysis time was too long and destroyed leukocytes — shorten it). For a same-day sample, adjust and re-run; for an older sample, reduce hemolysis time and consider washing more than once.
09

Troubleshooting

Every hardware error on BriCyte follows the same three-step ladder: Remove & retry → Restart the cytometer → Contact Mindray Customer Service. What differs is which specific check to make first. Errors group into three families by their code prefix.

9.1 · Fluidics & sample errors (2xxxx)

SymptomFirst check
Sheath / waste aspiration or discharge abnormalRemove & retry, then restart. Persistent waste-discharge errors: run Maintenance → Prime Sheath Filter first.
Flow sensor abnormalCheck sample volume is sufficient and free of excess bubbles, re-run; if it recurs, run Clean Flow Cell 1–3×.
Sample probe / flow cell cloggedCheck for particulates or bubbles in the sample; run Unclog Sampling Channel or Unclog Flow Cell 1–3×.
Sheath tubing emptyCheck the sheath inlet connector on the reagent carriage is tight; run Prime Bubble Filter 1–3×.
Insufficient sheath / waste container fullReplace the sheath container, or empty the waste container — do not try to run the instrument past either alarm.
Ambient / sheath temperature abnormalConfirm room temperature is within 15–32°C before retrying.

9.2 · Optics & laser errors (32xxx / 33xxx)

Laser and APD-detector-box temperature/power errors (red, blue and violet lasers each have their own set of codes) share one first check: confirm ambient temperature is within 15–32°C, click Remove, and retry. If a laser power or temperature error persists after a restart, it needs Mindray service — do not attempt to open the optical box beyond confirming it is fully closed (an “optical box open” error is the one case that’s user-resolvable: close it and retry).

9.3 · Loading / mechanical errors (4xxxx)

Unloading or carousel-handling errors: Remove & retry, then restart; check the carousel is seated correctly and no tube is obstructing the tube-access door before calling for service.

Reading an error

The error dialog always shows the most recent error first, with its own troubleshooting text; select any listed error to see its specific instructions. “Mute Alarm” only silences the beep — it does not clear the error. “Remove” clears errors that are auto-clearable; anything else needs the listed corrective action first.

9.4 · Assay-level troubleshooting (not an instrument fault)

What you seeLikely causeWhat to do
Whole plot shifted/spread, not one populationFluidic instability — air bubble, sample run dry, or a blockage that resolved itselfRe-run the tube; if it recurs on multiple samples, degas/clean the flow cell
CD45/SSC clean, but CD3/CD4/CD8 plots poorly separatedResidual protein/debris interfering with antibody resolutionSheath-fluid wash & re-suspend protocol, §7.3
CD4%+CD8% vs CD3% deviates >10%Atypical T-cell subset, or a gating errorRe-check gates first (§7.1); if gates are correct, follow the double-positive/negative interpretation in §7.2
T-tube and BNK-tube CD3% disagree >5%Usually a tube mix-up, not biologyVerify tube labelling and re-test before reporting
Diagonal “smear” between two colour channels rather than square quadrantsCompensation not set, or set incorrectlyRe-run auto setup with fresh QC beads; review the compensation matrix (0–200% input range)
Poor CV / scattered populations on QC beadsBubbles in the flow cell or fluidics lineMaintenance → Degas Flow Cell or Degas Fluidics System
9A

Troubleshooting map

One page that links what you see on the instrument to why it happens and what to do. Actions come from the Operator’s Manual (§10.3 and §11) and the sections of this guide; the principle column is explanation from §1.

How to use this map

Read it left to right: what you see (symptom), why it happens (principle), what to do (action). The principle matters because it tells you which group of fixes to try first. A problem that hits every plot at once is almost always the instrument side (fluids, light). A problem in one marker or one population is almost always the sample or the set-up.

Every error follows the same ladder: Remove & retry → Restart → Contact Mindray. “Mute Alarm” only silences the beep; it does not clear the error.

9A.1 · Symptom map

AreaSymptomPrinciple (why)Action
FluidicsSheath or waste aspiration / discharge abnormal (2xxxx)The sheath stream carries every cell past the laser. If it cannot be drawn or drained steadily, flow is unstable.Click Remove and retry → restart the cytometer. For repeated waste-discharge errors run Prime Sheath Filter. Still failing → Mindray.
FluidicsFlow sensor abnormalThe flow sensor measures what the sample is doing. Low sample volume, bubbles or a dirty flow cell upset its reading.Check there is enough sample without bubbles and re-run. If it recurs, run Clean Flow Cell 1–3× (needs ≥1 mL Probe Cleanser diluted 1:10, in the holder or carousel position 20).
FluidicsSample probe or flow cell cloggedCells are squeezed into a very thin stream (hydrodynamic focusing, §1.2). Particles or clots block that narrow path.Look for clots, debris or bubbles in the tube. Run Unclog Sampling Channel or Unclog Flow Cell, 1–3×.
FluidicsSheath tubing empty, or bubbles after the sheath ran outAir in the fluid path breaks the steady laminar flow the optics rely on.Check the sheath inlet connector on the reagent carriage is tight. Run Prime Bubble Filter 1–3×; Initialize Fluidics System also resets after run-dry (and is a weekly job).
FluidicsEvery plot shifts or spreads at onceOne cause upstream of all plots: unstable flow, usually a bubble or a tube that ran dry. It is not one population misbehaving.Re-run, do not re-gate. If it repeats on several samples, run Degas Flow Cell / Degas Fluidics System.
FluidicsPoor CV, scattered populations or high background on QC beadsBeads should give tight spots. Bubbles or dirt in the flow cell widen the signal.Degas Flow Cell or Degas Fluidics System; Clean Flow Cell after a heavy sample day. Then repeat auto setup (§6.1).
OpticsLaser or detector-box temperature / power error (32xxx, 33xxx)Lasers and detectors work only inside a temperature window.Confirm room temperature is 15–32°C, click Remove, retry. “Optical box open”: close it and retry. Persisting after restart → Mindray; do not open the optics.
Set-upAuto setup fails for a laser or channelThe software could not bring the bead signal to its target values. Bad bead prep or an active error are common causes.Make sure no error is showing and the beads were prepared that day, in the dark. Retry. Keeps failing → Mindray recalibrates. No patient samples on a failed setup (§6.1).
Set-upDiagonal smear between two colour channels instead of square quadrantsLight from one dye leaks into the neighbouring detector. Compensation removes it; wrong values leave a diagonal smear.Re-run auto setup with fresh QC beads, then review the compensation matrix (0–200%).
CountAbsolute counts differ from the reference or QC, and the instrument is otherwise normalThe count factor converts events into cells/µL. It can shift after a major part is replaced or long storage.Follow the calibration refresh in §6A (50–150% allowed). Rule out sample mixing and tube volume first.
SampleCD45/SSC is clean but CD3, CD4, CD8 are poorly separatedLeftover protein or debris in the tube interferes with antibody resolution.Sheath-fluid wash and re-suspend, then re-acquire (§7.3).
SampleT-tube and BNK-tube CD3% disagree by more than 5%Biology rarely explains this. A tube mix-up usually does.Verify tube labelling and re-test before reporting.
AnalysisCD4% + CD8% differs from CD3% by more than 10%Either an unusual T-cell subset or a gate in the wrong place.Check the gates first (§7.1). If they are correct, follow the double-positive / double-negative interpretation (§7.2).
MechanicalLoading or unloading error, carousel problem (4xxxx)The tube must be in the right place for the probe to reach it.Remove & retry, restart. Check the carousel is seated and no tube blocks the tube-access door.

9A.2 · Error groups at a glance

The manual’s error list (Table 11-1) has 152 codes of 8 digits. They fall into seven groups by the first two digits. The group names are my reading of the messages, not manual headings.

Fluidics

24 codes · 21–23xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: sheath and waste aspiration or discharge, pressures, flow sensor, clogged probe or flow cell, empty sheath tubing, sheath low, waste full, reagent carriage, ambient and sheath temperature.
  • Usually: Remove & retry → restart → Mindray (10 codes).
  • Specific fixes: flow sensor → check sample volume and bubbles, Clean Flow Cell 1–3×; probe clog → Unclog Sampling Channel; flow cell clog → Unclog Flow Cell; sheath tubing empty → tighten the inlet connector, Fluidics Bubble Remove 1–3×; sheath low → replace sheath; waste full → empty it; 5 temperature codes → room 15–32°C; reagent carriage → clear foreign matter.

Lasers & optics

29 codes · 32–33xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: optical box open; red, blue and violet laser temperature, temperature sensor and power; optical temperature sensor; red, blue and violet APD detector box temperature.
  • Temperature too high or low (15 codes): confirm room temperature 15–32°C, Remove & retry.
  • Sensor and power errors (13 codes): Remove & retry → restart → Mindray.
  • Optical box open: close it and retry.

Loading & carousel

27 codes · 41, 42, 51, 52, 68

  • Goes wrong: loading and unloading, probe wipe, carousel, autoloader motors, electromagnet, 96-well tray, plus set-up mismatches.
  • Mechanical (11 codes): Remove & retry → restart → Mindray.
  • You can fix: autoloader door open (9 codes) → close it; carousel or 96-well tray missing → put it in; tube not detected → place a tube; carousel ID mismatch → match worklist and carousel No.; no free position → take out a tube; wrong autoloader type setting; sample aspiration abnormal → make sure the tube has enough sample.

Electronics

29 codes · 63xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: driver board, laser board and main control board voltage, high-voltage supply.
  • Do: Remove & retry. If it stays, call Mindray. The manual lists no user fix for these.

Acquisition & QC

20 codes · 66xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: communication (12 codes), machine type or component version mismatch, pulse identification, data acquisition, processing speed, FSC voltage, QC status.
  • Communication and most others: Remove & retry → restart → Mindray.
  • Machine type not matched: software was reinstalled or connected to another cytometer → reset machine type, restart. Component version: Mindray.
  • Processing speed too high: raise a too-low threshold, dilute a concentrated sample, lower the flow rate, check the PC network link.
  • QC expired: run Auto Setup on the QC screen. QC failed: prepare the sample again and re-acquire.

Startup

16 codes · 67xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: startup, startup after pack-up, shutdown, pack-up and standby procedures not finished; startup temperature control timeout (6 codes); workflow interrupted.
  • Usually: clear other errors first, then Remove & retry; or the standard ladder (7 codes).
  • Interrupted pack-up: restart and repeat Startup after Pack-up (or Pack-up and Shutdown). Interrupted shutdown: power off directly.

Self-test

7 codes · 69xxxxxx

  • Goes wrong: filter, tubing tightness, sheath ceramic pump, red, blue and violet laser, warm-up system self-tests.
  • Do first: remove any other error, then repeat the self-test.
  • Filter: De-gas Fluidics. Tubing tightness: Prime Filter, De-gas Fluidics, Fluidics Initialization. Pump: standard ladder. Lasers and warm-up: Mindray if it persists.
Stop and call Mindray when

A laser power or temperature error survives a restart; a fluidics error survives Remove & retry, restart and the listed maintenance program; auto setup keeps failing; or pipes and fluidic parts look worn (stop using the instrument). Do not run patient samples while any of these is unresolved.

Sources: Operator’s Manual Table 11-1 (error list), §10.3 (maintenance programs, timing and purpose), §11.2 (error ladder), §9.2 (auto setup), §6.2.4 (count factor); assay rows from this guide’s §9.4.

10

Maintenance schedule

All routine maintenance runs from System → Maintenance. Most items are “as needed”, triggered by a specific symptom rather than a fixed calendar — the exceptions are the weekly fluidics initialization and the 6-monthly filter change.

ProgramRun it when…Frequency
Degas flow cellAbnormal population distribution, high background noise, poor QC CVAs needed
Degas fluidics systemScattered populations, high background noise, poor QC CVAs needed
Clean flow cellPoor optical signal, scattered populations, flow sensor abnormal, or after a heavy sample dayAs needed
Initialize fluidics systemAbnormal distribution, bubbles from a sheath run-dry event, or after connecting/replacing fluidic partsEvery week
Unclog flow cell“Flow cell clogged” errorAs needed
Unclog sampling channel“Sample probe clogged” errorAs needed
Prime sheath filterAfter replacing the sheath container (contamination/bubbles) or the sheath filter itselfAs needed
Prime bubble filterAfter replacing the bubble filterAs needed
Pack-up & shutdown / startup after pack-upInstrument will be idle for an extended periodAs needed
Replace sheath fluid containerInsufficient / exhausted / expired / contaminatedAs needed
Replace waste containerFullDaily or as needed
Replace filtersPast service life, or repeated self-test failuresEvery 6 months or as needed
Clean the coverVisible contamination, or a reagent/sample spillAs needed

Cleaning the cover

Recommended: 75% ethyl alcohol. Prohibited: 3% hydrogen peroxide (corrodes metal), Aerodesin 2000, Cidex OPA. Wear gloves, lab coat and eye protection — every surface and component is treated as potentially infectious.

Replacing sheath/waste containers

Never mix a new sheath fluid container with residue from the old one — it corrupts the volume measurement. Only detach the waste cap assembly when the power indicator is steady (not flickering), to avoid overflow.

Logs

The System → Log screen keeps 2 years of error and operation logs (oldest overwritten once full) — filterable by date, error ID/level, or log type, and exportable to PC. This is usually the fastest way to reconstruct what happened before an intermittent fault, and worth pulling before calling Mindray support.

11

Reagents & consumables

Composition, storage and handling notes for every fluid this panel touches.

11.1 · CD3‑FITC/CD8‑PE/CD45‑PerCP/CD4‑APC reagent

Active ingredients, 1 mL / 50 tests
CD3‑FITC antibody (clone SK7)<10 μg/mL
CD8‑PE antibody (clone SK1)<10 μg/mL
CD45‑PerCP antibody (clone 2D1)<10 μg/mL
CD4‑APC antibody (clone SK3)<10 μg/mL
Phosphate buffer<0.3%
Protein protective agent<0.3%
Preservative0.1%
Stabilizer<10%

Store at 2–8°C, protected from light, container closed when not in use. Unopened shelf life 18 months; once opened, 90 days at 2–8°C. Transport cold with ice packs. Never freeze. Discard on any visible precipitation or discoloration — both indicate instability or deterioration.

11.2 · Lysing solution

10× concentrate; active ingredients diethylene glycol (≤40%) and formaldehyde (≤15%) — treat as hazardous (H302/H312/H314/H317/H332/H351: harmful if swallowed/in contact with skin/inhaled, causes severe skin and eye burns, may cause an allergic skin reaction, suspected carcinogen). Wear gloves and eye protection; work in a ventilated area; rinse thoroughly and seek medical advice on skin or eye contact.

Dilute 1:10 with distilled/deionized water immediately before use (10× concentrate : water = 1:9). Diluted 1× solution is stable 30 days at 20–25°C. Concentrate: store 2–25°C, unopened shelf life 2 years, opened stability 6 months.

Two protocols exist: Lyse/No‑Wash (450 μL 1× solution into 50 μL blood+antibody, 15 min dark incubation, run directly — this is the protocol used for the routine CD3/CD4/CD8/CD45 panel) and Lyse/Wash (2 mL 1× solution into 100 μL blood+antibody, 10 min incubation, centrifuge/wash twice with PBS — used where a washed, more stable preparation is needed). Nucleated red blood cells resist lysis — expect incomplete red-cell clearing in myelofibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, thalassaemia and spherocytosis specimens.

11.3 · Sheath fluid

An electrically conducting, fluorescence-free buffer (phosphate buffer ≤0.5%, sodium chloride ≤1%, preservative ≤0.3%) that forms the carrier stream for every sample. Store 2–32°C; unopened shelf life 2 years; opened stability 60 days at 15–32°C. Never freeze. If blank-count results look abnormal after shipping, let the container sit at room temperature 24 h before use.

11.4 · QC particles

SPHERO™ Rainbow Fluorescent Particles, single population, 3.0–3.5 μm, ≈10×10&sup6; particles/mL in deionized water with 0.02% sodium azide / 0.01% NP40, excitable 365–650 nm. Store at room temperature unopened; 2–8°C after first use; protect from light; never freeze. Shake or vortex briefly before every use; dilution 1–2 drops per 1 mL gives an adequate event rate. Diluted particles keep refrigerated but expire one year after the vial is first opened — write the opening date on the bottle.

11.5 · Probe cleanser

Dilute 1:10 with distilled water before use. Used during the Clean Flow Cell maintenance routine and at shutdown (≥3 mL per cycle).

11.6 · Consumables

ItemSpec
Standard flow tube12±0.4 mm ø × 75±2 mm, wall 1±0.15 mm — auto or manual loading

12

Lab-user FAQ

The questions hospital lab staff actually ask on a support call, answered from the source documentation.

“My CD4%+CD8% doesn’t add up to CD3%. Is the machine broken?”

Not necessarily. A 5–10% deviation is expected and normal. Beyond that, it’s a signal to look at the CD4–CD8 plot for an atypical population (double-positive or double-negative cells) before assuming an instrument fault — see §7.2.

“Can I use PBS or saline instead of distilled water to dilute the lysing solution?”

No. Isotonic solutions will not lyse red cells — the lysing step specifically depends on the hypotonic shock from distilled/deionized water. Use isotonic solutions only for the wash step (sheath fluid, saline or PBS), never for lysing.

“Do I need to run QC beads before every batch, or just once a day?”

Once per day, before the first patient sample — but re-run it any time you have reason to doubt the instrument (an error was just cleared, a filter was replaced, a laser fault occurred), not only on a fixed clock.

“The plots are diagonal-smeared instead of square. What’s wrong?”

That’s the visual signature of a compensation problem, not a biological or gating one. Re-run QC/auto setup with fresh beads and check the compensation matrix before re-gating anything.

“Can I refrigerate the blood sample before staining if I’m running behind?”

No — refrigeration before staining is specifically called out as a source of aberrant results. Keep the specimen at room temperature (20–25°C) and stain within 48 h of draw.

“Why is my HLA-B27 result showing ‘Undetermined’?”

The software couldn’t separate lymphocytes from debris on the FSC‑SSC plot. Try manually re-circling the lymphocyte population first; if that’s genuinely not possible, check whether the tube looks reddish (incomplete lysis) or whether cell counts look unusually low (hemolysis ran too long) — see §8.3.

“A patient’s blood is very lipemic/jaundiced/haemolysed — should I run it anyway?”

No. These are explicitly listed interfering conditions that can yield incorrect results (bilirubin and chylomicrons both interfere with the assay). Request a redraw where clinically possible rather than reporting an unreliable result.

“Can I mix reagents or QC material from different manufacturers on this instrument?”

No — the cytometer, reagents and controls are validated as one system. Mixed-supplier use is explicitly called out as a cause of degraded performance and unreliable results.

“Why does the lab need to set its own reference range instead of using the one in this guide?”

The published ranges (§3.5) come from one population (China, ages 18–65) using one preparative technique. Gender, age, ethnicity and local technique can all shift where “normal” sits — the manufacturer explicitly asks each laboratory to verify or establish its own range rather than adopt the insert value unchanged.

Glossary & instrument specs

Terms as used throughout this guide, and the platform specifications worth having on hand for a site survey or a service call.

13.1 · Glossary

FSC / SSCForward / side scatter — size and internal-complexity signals collected from every particle
CompensationMathematical correction removing one fluorochrome’s spectral spillover from another detector’s channel
GateA drawn region isolating a population of interest for downstream analysis
Quadrant / cross gateA two-axis gate splitting a plot into four regions — double-negative, two single-positives, double-positive
MESFMolecules of equivalent soluble fluorochrome — the unit used to state fluorescence sensitivity
MFIMean/median fluorescence intensity
Lyse/No‑WashStain, lyse, run directly — no centrifugation step; the routine protocol for this panel
Lyse/WashStain, lyse, centrifuge and resuspend in PBS — used when a washed, more stable prep is required
Levey‑JenningsA control chart plotting QC results against target ±SD lines over time
Absolute countCells per microlitre, as opposed to a percentage of a gated population
TBNKT-cell / B-cell / NK-cell lymphocyte subset panel
Isotype controlAn antibody of matched class but irrelevant specificity, used to gauge non-specific/background binding (used in HLA‑B27, not in the routine T-cell panel)

13.3 · Reading this guide onward

This page draws only on the BriCyte MX/MC Operator’s Manual, the CD4 panel and companion reagent Instructions For Use, the vendor training material, the Melbourne Cytometry Platform primer and the laboratory’s own SOP — nothing was pulled from outside sources. Where a revision date, a validity window, or a software label differs between documents (noted inline where it occurs), treat the reagent’s own current-lot Instructions For Use and your site’s current MRFlow software version as the authority, and update this reference accordingly.
